newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan's Taleban consolidate airbase gains.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan's Taleban consolidate airbase gains.

text.p: Jubilant Taleban fighters tightened their grip on a newly captured airbase and town north of the Afghan capital Kabul on Friday, witnesses said.
The Taleban seized the big Soviet-built airbase of Bagram and the town of Charikar, about 50 km (30 miles) from Kabul, in a dawn attack on Thursday that apparently met little resistance.

Taleban fighters and travellers interviewed on Friday at this village, 30 km (19 miles) south of Bagram, said there had been little overnight fighting and the front line was now about two km (one mile) north of Charikar, now largely deserted.
A spokesman for the ousted government's military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, quoted by Iranian television, denied on Thursday that Bagram had fallen or that the front lines had moved.
But witnesses said Charikar, on the main road to the Salang Pass connecting Kabul and the Shomali Valley with northern Afghanistan, was firmly in Taleban hands.
They said the town was relatively unscarred, suggesting it had fallen with little struggle.
Witnesses also said the Taleban were in full control of Bagram airbase, where bearded fighters were celebrating with bursts of gunfire from assault rifles and machineguns.
The base, on a dusty plain with snow-capped peaks in the background, was used by Soviet forces in the 1980s to support a communist-backed government in Kabul.
Military analysts said the latest Taleban victory was significant, lifting the purist Islamic movement's morale, but had not necessarily dealt the opposition alliance a killer blow.
"There doesn't seem to have been much close-quarter fighting or determined opposition," said a foreign military observer.

"The anti-Taleban forces seem to have withdrawn after coming under artillery fire, possibly indicating low morale or lack of logistic resoruces. But it could signal a change in strategy to stretch the Taleban and use guerrilla tactics against them."

Masood, forced to flee to his native Panjsher Valley after the Taleban seized Kabul on September 27, used such tactics successfully during a counter-attack in October that brought his forces back to within 20 km (13 miles) of the capital.
He helped the well-armed, mainly ethnic Tajik population of the Shomali Valley mount ambushes against the Taleban from villages, vineyards and orchards along the road to the north.
Taleban fighters in village bazaars risked being stabbed in the back, blinded or burned to death, local people say. The Taleban responded by burning down houses or rocketing villages.

But forces loyal to Masood and his rival-turned-ally General Abdul Rasheed Dostum failed to break through Taleban defences around Kabul, just as the Islamic fighters had earlier failed to penetrate Dostum's northern heartland beyond the Hindu Kush moutain range or Masood's Panjsher redoubt.
Taleban leaders sent messages that offered local people, who were running short of food with the approach of winter, an amensty if they stopped the rebellion.
That brought a lull of nearly two months, broken abruptly by Thursday's offensive, and launched the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan, often a time for truce.
Military analysts said it would be harder now for Masood to mobilise armed civilians against the Taleban in the Shomali Valley, partly because so many people have now fled the area.
"I wouldn't place too many bets on a new uprising, but Masood is a master of guerrilla operations," one said.

The Taleban, seeking to impose their strict vision of Islamic Shaira law throughout Afghanistan, moved onto the offensive just one day after three days of U.N.-sponsored peace talks with the opposition ended inconclusively in Islamabad.
Military observers say their latest advances might indicate poor coordination among the opposition alliance -- Masood's Tajik, Dostum's Uzbeks and a Shi'ite Moslem militia.
The Taleban now control up to three-quarters of Afghanistan, but have so far found it hard to consolidate their hold on areas outside their mainly Pashtun native provinces in the south.
